title: Urban Heat Interventions and Emergency Admission Risk

manuscript.abstract: We evaluate cooling corridors and shaded transit stops as practical interventions for reducing heat-related emergency admissions in dense urban districts. The study compares intervention and control neighborhoods across two summer periods and reports statistically significant differences in admissions and surface temperature.
manuscript.methods: Neighborhoods were matched on age distribution, tree canopy, income, and historic admissions. Intervention areas received cooling corridors, shaded transit stops, and public hydration stations. The analysis uses difference-in-differences with a prespecified endpoint, randomized block assignment for pilot corridors, and sensitivity checks for smoke-event days.
manuscript.results: Intervention districts showed lower mean surface temperature and fewer heat-related emergency admissions during the trial period. The strongest result appears near shaded transit stops. The manuscript currently claims the intervention prevents admissions across all hot days.
manuscript.limitations: The pilot spans two summers and may not generalize to coastal districts. Sensor gaps occurred during one smoke event.
